God damn that JSON is stupid for an API. Every row is a string of shit you have to parse again, which isn't valid JSON itself? I could understand if the string format is there to be performant elsewhere, perhaps using a string field to store the record and displaying that record directly to users without having multiple database rows, or some such. But for an API? Damn.

could have been:

{
[ "user" : "blah", "reason" : "blah", "by" : "username", "on" : "[datestring] | unix timestamp" ],
[ "user" : "blah", "reason" : "blah", "by" : "username", "on" : "[datestring] | unix timestamp" ],
...
[ "user" : "blah", "reason" : "blah", "by" : "username", "on" : "[datestring] | unix timestamp" ]
}

That would allow you to treat the string as a block of JSON and get at the fields directly without having to re-parse each row manually.

Now, even that is kind of dumb, but the price of using JSON or JS, evar.

Look at all that wasted data repeating "username" for every column. This is the fault of JS's silly design... meh.

If I have to parse this crap to use in a program, I'm gonna transform it.

{ [ 
[ "banee", "reason", "mod", "timestamp" ],
[ "SomeFuckhead", "didn't follow rule", "Atko", "2/14/2016 1:23:45" ],
[ "SomeFuckhead", "didn't follow rule and stole my GF", "Atko", "2/14/2016 13:45:56" ],
...
[ "SomeFuckhead", "didn't follow rule", "Atko", "2/14/2016 13:45:56" ]
] }

Ah now, that's better. no more stupid repeating the field name for each field's data. The first record #0 gives the order and names of the fields for the subsequent rows. This also allows you to very quickly output tables without re-parsing each entry, etc. Not to mention the above JSON encoding for tabular data is universal, the same block of code that generates one table view of that data woud generate a table for any other encoded record set the API could throw at you.

A good beautifier would then also align your columns for you.

{[[ "banee", "reason", "mod", "timestamp" ],
 [ "SomeFuckhead", "didn't follow rule", "Atko", "2/14/2016 1:23:45" ],
 [ "SomeFuckhead", "didn't follow rule and stole my GF", "Atko", "2/14/2016 13:45:56" ],
...
 [ "SomeFuckhead", "didn't follow rule", "Atko", "2/14/2016 1:23:45" ]
]}

Now, maybe the database doesn't use that silly formatting internally, and a whack coder had to manually want to make it harder for themselves, meh, beats the shit out of me. It's not putt's fault, that's for sure.

TL;DR: API a shit, mang. Too late to fix nao. Can see why Atko would find an excuse to bale. Positive side: Site has much room to become far more performant. Negative Side: Making shit better will break all existing code that uses API.

Do you run an NAS or Personal Cloud? What kind, why, and does it work for you?
I have a FrankeNAS using FreeNAS. It uses old ribbon cables and a really old x64 processor. I wanted to be able to back up my computers in case I have a hard drive failure.

I have a personal cloud hosted on Digital Ocean Linux servers. I have Apache configured to only respond to http requests within my virtual network. Each server and client computer is a Tinc node. The cloud itself is OwnCloud. I hope to eventually add encrypted email and music streaming. It's pretty good except that you really have to stay on top of your patches. Been compromised once but they didn't get to anything interesting before I discovered it.

I use Open-PFS (a very simple open source file server which runs on top of PHP+Apache+Linux, allowing you to use your server for other thing as well e.g. VPN) http://www.panhost.xyz/public/open-pfs-lap-1.3.zip

My server www.panhost.xyz runs on a VPS from BuyVM. Running your own server to share images and such pretty much lets you make the rules and stays online as long as you pay your hosting bills. So far works great for me and a couple friends who have posted things on my server (including /u/lei_feng67).
Why run a server when you can just have a shitload of external HDDs?

I have 6 drives in a RAID under ZFS running on Ubuntu Server (12.04 I think) running on an old server that was slated for recycling. Coming on 2 years of uptime so far, which isn't really that remarkable for Linux (at my old job we had a Red Hat server that had been up for 6 years and even then the only reason it got powered down was we moved the server room).

Prior to this I'd always used hardware RAID controllers and not only were they expensive but I was vulnerable to controller failure. After 10 years good luck finding the exact same board with the same revision level. But after trying ZFS I'd never go back unless there was a very compelling reason.

This server replaced a couple of DLink DNS-320s that I was using for storage. One of them failed taking all the data with it. Not a single regret since switching to ZFS.
